pages.title: The variable speed drive
pages.for: Setting a cage motor's speed, and starting it with no inrush. It turns the supply into DC, then builds AC at the frequency it is asked for. Up to base speed, the voltage moves in step.
pages.rule:
ns = 120 × f ÷ p
Volts per hertz constant up to base speed: 400 V ÷ 50 Hz = 8 V per Hz
Fan or pump power goes with speed cubed

Below base speed: constant flux. Above it: the volts stop at rated and the flux falls.
DC bus about 1.35 × supply volts: about 540 V DC on 400 V.
Common trips: overcurrent, earth fault, overvoltage on a fast stop, input phase loss.
A ship's motor on 440 V, 60 Hz: 440 ÷ 60 = 7.33 V per Hz, and base speed is 60 Hz.

traps.text: Above base speed the volts stop rising. The flux falls, and so does the torque it can give. Yet a fan at 60 Hz needs 1.2³ = 1.73 times its 50 Hz power. Check the motor and the load can take the whole speed range.
traps.cite: [^7] [^8] [^18] [^2] ABB ACS580 technical eBook; ABB ACS800-37 hardware manual

traps.text: The big savings come on fans and pumps. Their power goes with speed cubed. Real systems save less.
traps.cite: [^2] [^9] US DOE motor tip sheet; ABB energy efficiency plan

traps.text: Isolate the whole drive, not just the door switch. Wait out its discharge time, 5 minutes on one maker's drive. Prove your tester. Then prove DC+ to DC−, each to earth, and the input and motor terminals dead. Charged, the bus holds about 540 V DC.
traps.cite: [^4] [^10] [^1] [^15] [^16] ABB ACS800-37 hardware manual; HSE GS38

traps.text: Disconnect the drive before you insulation test the motor or its cable.
Overvoltage on a fast stop means the load is driving the motor. Lengthen the deceleration time or fit a brake chopper.
traps.cite: [^13] [^14] Eaton fault codes; ABB ACS880-01 hardware manual

pages.where: Pumps, fans and compressors to save energy. Cranes, winches, bow thrusters and ventilation at sea. Anywhere the speed must be set.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A four-pole motor runs on 50 Hz. How fast does its field turn?
pages.why: 120 × 50 ÷ 4 = 1500 rpm. The shaft runs a little below it. Change the frequency and that speed changes. That is how a drive sets speed.

pages.name: How it works
pages.text:
A drive sets a motor's speed by setting its frequency.

The rectifier turns the incoming AC into DC. Capacitors on the [[DC bus]] smooth it. On 400 V the bus sits at about 400 × 1.35 = 540 V DC.

The inverter switches that DC on and off very fast. It varies the width of the pulses to build AC at the frequency and voltage it is asked for.

The field turns at 120 × f ÷ p. Lower f, and the field and the rotor slow down together.
pages.alt: Rectifier DC bus Inverter Motor Supply 400 V, 50 Hz about 540 V DC M chosen frequency, matching voltage

pages.name: Volts per hertz
pages.text: Below 50 Hz the voltage falls with the frequency, 8 V for every hertz. At 40 Hz the drive gives 320 V and the field turns at 1200 rpm. The volts per hertz stay at 8, so the flux stays at rated. Held at 400 V instead, 40 Hz would give 10 V per hertz. That asks for a quarter more flux, and the iron saturates. Above 50 Hz the voltage stays at 400 V. At 60 Hz the field turns at 1800 rpm and the flux falls to 83%.

So the flux stays at rated, and the field turns at 1200 rpm. 50 Hz is the motor's base speed. The stator is a winding on iron, like a transformer. Its flux goes with the volts per hertz. Example motor: 400 V, 50 Hz, four poles. The arrow turns 100 times slower than the real field.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: The drive runs this 400 V, 50 Hz motor at 25 Hz. What voltage does it give?
pages.why: 400 ÷ 50 = 8 V per hertz. 8 × 25 = 200 V. The volts per hertz stay at 8, so the flux stays at rated. The field turns at 120 × 25 ÷ 4 = 750 rpm.

pages.name: How it behaves
pages.text:
Speed: Set by the frequency. The shaft runs a little below 120 × f ÷ p.

Starting: The drive ramps up the frequency. No inrush and no jolt.

Below base speed: Constant flux. The motor can give its rated torque if it stays cool.

Above base speed: [[Field weakening]]. The volts stay at rated, so the flux falls. The power it can give stays about constant, so the torque it can give falls.

Low speed: A self-cooled motor's fan slows too, so it cannot carry rated torque for long.

pages.name: Where it is used
pages.text:
Used for: Pumps and fans, to save energy, and anything whose speed must be set.

At sea: Cranes, winches, bow thrusters, ventilation, pumps, compressors and propulsion.

Savings: Fan and pump power goes with speed cubed. Real systems save less.

Limits: Drives are the main source of harmonics at sea. NATO warship rules cap voltage distortion at 5%. Fast pulses can also drive current through the bearings and wear them.

pages.name: Faults and tests
pages.text:
Safety first: A cabinet's door switch may leave the input busbars live, so isolate the whole drive. Wait out its discharge time, 5 minutes on one maker's drive. Prove your tester. Then prove the DC bus, input and motor terminals dead.

Insulation test: Disconnect the drive first. The tester can damage it.

Overcurrent: A short, earth fault, loose joint or jammed load.

Earth fault: Often damp insulation.

Input phase loss: A blown fuse or loose input lead.

Restarts by itself: An auto-reset drive can restart without warning. Label it.

pages.name: Find the fault
pages.task: A drive on a big fan trips on overvoltage every time the fan is stopped quickly. Running, it is fine. What is the likely cause?
pages.answer: The fan drives the motor as it slows, pushing energy into the DC bus
pages.why: The drive drops the frequency fast, but the heavy fan cannot slow that quickly. So the rotor runs faster than the field. The motor becomes a generator and pushes energy back into the DC bus. The bus voltage rises until the drive trips. One maker's 400 V drive trips at 840 V. Lengthen the deceleration time, or fit a brake chopper and resistor.
options: The fan drives the motor as it slows, pushing energy into the DC bus
The fan is overloaded and the motor draws too much current
The supply has lost a phase and the bus sags
